newsitem.title: UK: Industry muted on Pru portfolio strategy.
newsitem.headline: Industry muted on Pru portfolio strategy.

text.p: A plan by Prudential Portfolio Managers (PPM) to allow it to hold potentially price-sensitive talks with companies in which it invests was innovative but could be difficult to implement, industry sources said.
They said the strategy proposed by PPM chairman David Higgs raised ethical questions and could unwittingly compromise credibility. PPM is the fund management arm of Prudential Corp.
Higgs told the Financial Times the group had set up a mechanism for companies in which it invests to hold advance discussions on possible deals or strategy shifts.
He said a "Chinese wall" between him and PPM fund managers would ensure the strategy worked, and would allow managers to continue trading in the shares of companies which chose to consult him.
Chinese walls are a convention to prevent price-sensitive information seeping between dealing, fund management and corporate finance operations within the same investment house.
Higgs has just sent an 18-page pamphlet outlining the policy to PPM clients.

"Within a single part of an organisation to try to put a Chinese Wall around himself is quite difficult if that person is also straddling (the wall)," Stephen Tanner, director general of the Institutional Fund Managers' Association, told Reuters.
"In most organisations these days you have Chinese walls and you have to have some people who straddle them. The question is really how much of a straddle they do.
"The more you can keep separate the activities on either side of the Chinese wall the better."
A director at a major UK fund management firm, who asked not to be identified, said the strategy did raise some difficulties, but was unlikely to be harmful if managed properly.
However, he said it would create tension with the advisers who normally consult on such issues with companies.
"What essentially they are doing is usurping their normal advisers' role and the advisers won't like that. Automatically that will create some friction."
He said difficulties included possible public criticism for any dealing in shares in which Higgs may have already have privileged information.
Also, Higgs' views may begin to exert undue influence on his fund managers' decisions.
No official regulatory approval appears to be necessary for the proposed PPM strategy, the fund manager said.
"But if anyone suspected that the Chinese walls did not work there would be hell to pay. As long as they did work then I don't see it as a problem."
Tanner said fund managers were under a clear obligation not to deal in shares of a company about which they had been consulted until the deal went public.

"What he (Higgs) is trying to avoid is that by saying I am chairman of the company, I don't do fund management. Therefore I can call myself the corporate financier and be on the other side of the wall'," Tanner said.
"I can see the logic in that. It is innovative. It is worth giving them some benefit of the doubt." But it did leave PPM open to possible criticism, he added.
Higgs would have to make clear that he never talked about shares because even if he knew nothing it would be assumed by fund managers that he did.

"If what he is telling you is that he is really basically a non-executive chairman of the fund management department, in the sense that he has nothing to do with fund management...then I suppose they could certainly try to get away with it."
